manifest.name: dsh-gui-browser
manifest.description: Operable live view of the Session's built-in Chromium in the GUI right Sidebar, with the viewer's input reported to the model

bundle.text:
# Operable live browser view for the GUI right Sidebar.
#
# `dsh-gui-browser` owns both halves: the Host watcher that attaches to each
# built-in Chromium's CDP port, pushes frames over a WebSocket, and translates
# the viewer's mouse, keyboard, IME, and clipboard input back into that same
# page; and the Client pane that draws it and takes that input.
#
# It has no browser of its own. A browser-use bundle enabled earlier in the
# layer order contributes the two provider rows (`browser-use`, which owns the
# single provider slot, and the Playwright MCP provider that fills it); this
# package depends on both provider packages so those rows resolve, and the
# override below points the provider at the platform launcher, which adds
# `--remote-debugging-port` beside Playwright's own control pipe.
#
# The override asserts the provider's package name as well as its id, so a
# profile that fills the slot with a different provider keeps it: the patch
# warns and is skipped, and the pane stays in its idle state instead of
# reconfiguring a browser it cannot drive. A matching override replaces
# `config` wholesale, so the provider's own fields are restated here.
#
# The launcher is named through `dshHomePath` rather than a path into this
# package, because the package's own location is not knowable from a patch: an
# installed bundle lives wherever its package manager put it. `launcher/install.mjs`
# (the bundle's postinstall) puts the right launcher for this platform in the
# registry directory both halves already agree on, so this expression is the only
# place either side has to know about the other.

- insert:
    - id: gui-browser
      name: 'dsh-gui-browser'

- id: browser-use-playwright-mcp
  name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-browser-use-playwright-mcp'
  config:
    mode: launch
    headless: true
    executablePath: !!js "dshHomePath('run', 'gui-browser', process.platform === 'win32' ? 'launcher.exe' : 'launcher.sh')"

readme.text:
An operable, live view of the Session's built-in Chromium in the GUI right
Sidebar — the same browser the model's `mcp__playwright-mcp__*` tools drive.

- **DSH 0.2.0-rc.2 or a later 0.2.x.** Declared twice — `engines.dsh` and the
  `@deepseek-ai/dsh-*` peers — so the plugin manager refuses the install on an
  older runtime and boot denies this row instead of failing halfway through;
  `dsh plugin allow-version` is the deliberate, per-version override.
- **Node** `^22.19 || >=24`.
- **A profile built on `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app`**:
  the pane is a Web right-Sidebar tab.
- **A browser-use bundle.** This package has no browser of its own. It depends on
  the provider packages (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-browser-use` and
  `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-browser-use-playwright-mcp`) so the provider rows
  resolve, and its patch overrides the Playwright MCP provider's row to point it
  at the launcher — but the rows themselves, and the isolated headless Chromium
  behind them, come from a browser-use bundle enabled earlier in the layer order
  (this repository's sibling `dsh-browser-use-playwright` is exactly those two
  rows). A profile admits **one** provider at a time: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-browser-use`
  owns the single registration slot and rejects a second one, so never enable two.
  Without any, the pane stays in

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-gui-browser
dsh --profile <profile> --dump-config   # the layer is listed as dsh-gui-browser
```

The package's `postinstall` (`launcher/install.mjs`) puts the platform launcher
in the registry directory; see [The launcher](#the-launcher). pnpm ≥10 runs no
dependency lifecycle script until it is allowed, so the install reports a pending
build script and the plugin manager asks for it — **approve it**, because without
that step there is no `launcher.sh`/`launcher.exe` for the provider to launch.
The step is idempotent and never fails an install: on a machine with no C#
compiler it warns loudly and leaves the Windows launcher absent rather than
breaking the package.

`dsh plugin --profile <profile> remove dsh-gui-browser` removes the dependency
and its layer.

**Installing into a running Harness needs a restart.** The plugin manager tries
to activate a newly installed bundle through HMR, but a Host answers plugin
specifiers from the package table it built at startup: a package name it has not
seen before is reported as `failed to import` and mounts only after a restart
(measured — the same process imports a pre-boot name, and the resolution a fresh
boot computes points at the right directory). The pane then appears on its own,
and the browser it mirrors keeps running across the restart because the browser's
debugging port is recorded in the registry directory rather than held by the
plugin. Replacing a package in place has the same requirement.

To publish from a checkout, `npm pack` builds the tarball; its contents are
exactly `files` in `package.json` — sources, the launcher's `.cs`/`.mjs`/`.sh`,
and never a compiled binary.

- **Same pixels as the model sees.** The Host half attaches to the browser
  Chromium was launched with (`--remote-debugging-port`, added by `wrapper.sh`)
  and pushes `Page.startScreencast` frames of the page target. Nothing is
  re-rendered, re-laid-out, or resized: the viewport, the page state, and the
  focus are whatever the browser has. One thing is corrected: a page Chromium
  created on its own (the new tab after a browser's last page closes, or a popup
  a site opened) is born at Chromium's unsized 800x600 default, which is narrower
  than most pages and arrives cropped, so any page still at exactly that size is
  set to the browser's own viewport (1280x720). Any other size — the model's own
  resize, a site's popup size — is left alone.
- **Frames only while somebody is watching.** Encoding a frame is the most
  expensive thing here, so frame production follows demand: it starts when a
  viewer attaches, stops when the last one detaches, and stops again while a
  viewer says its window is hidden. A hidden pane is sent no frames at all.
- **One shown page at a time.** A browser with several tabs paints all of them;
  casting every one is what once made the pane alternate b

| Route | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /gui-browser/list` | every live browser's state |
| `GET /gui-browser/status?port=` | one browser's state |
| `GET /gui-browser/frame.jpg?port=` | newest frame as a still image |
| `GET /gui-browser/activity?session=` | the exact text the model would receive |
| `GET /gui-browser/stream?port=` | MJPEG fallback for a non-WebSocket viewer |
| `POST /gui-browser/input?port=&session=` | the same commands the socket takes |
| `WS /gui-browser/ws` | frames and state downstream; input, caret, page choice, frame quality, and pane visibility upstream |

- `host.js` — stable entry; imports `engine.js?rev=<mtime>` so a Host-process
  module cache cannot pin an old generation for the life of the process.
- `engine.js` — registry watcher, CDP plumbing, WebSocket transport, input
  translation, and the model-facing activity record.
- `client.js` — the `gui-browser` right-Sidebar tab: canvas view, socket,
  pointer/keyboard/IME handling, zoom, auto-open.
- `wrapper.sh` — the POSIX Chromium launcher: allocates a free debugging port per
  launch and publishes it under `~/.dsh/run/gui-browser/`.
- `launcher/launcher.cs`, `launcher/install.mjs` — the same launcher for Windows
  and the install step that puts either one in place.

Playwright is pointed at a launcher through the provider's `executablePath`,
because that is the only hook a bundle has for adding `--remote-debugging-port`
beside Playwright's own control channel. The patch names it as
`dshHomePath('run', 'gui-browser', 'launcher.exe' | 'launcher.sh')`, so it never
has to know where the package was installed, and the bundle's `postinstall`
(`launcher/install.mjs`) puts the right launcher for the platform in that
directory:

- POSIX: `wrapper.sh` copied to `launcher.sh`, mode 755.
- Windows: `launcher.cs` compiled to `launcher.exe` by the `csc.exe` that every
  .NET Framework install provides, with PowerShell `Add-Type` as the fallback.
  Nothing prebuilt ships in the package, so there is nothing to sign or build per
  architecture; a machine with no C# compiler is reported loudly and otherwise
  ignored, and the model keeps its browser either way.

Two things about the Windows launcher are load-bearing. Playwright spawns
`executablePath` **without a shell**, so a `.cmd` cannot be used at all
(`spawn EINVAL`); and it hands the browser its DevTools pipe as *CRT file
descriptors* 3 and 4, which Windows passes in `STARTUPINFO.lpReserved2` — a
per-process descriptor table the child's CRT reads at startup. The launcher
therefore calls `CreateProcess` itself, forwards that block unchanged, and marks
the handles it names inheritable; `Process.Start` would lose the block and
Chromium would refuse to start with "Remote debugging pipe file descriptors are
not open". `launcher.exe --gui-browser-handles` prints the inherited table, which
is how that failure is told apart from a broken browser.

- Ctrl+wheel (page zoom) is not forwarded: it would desync the pane's geometry
  from the browser's viewport.
- A browser showing this GUI itself is view-only, so the nested panel cannot
  forward its own clicks forever.
- The viewer's clipboard reaches the page on paste, and the page's selection
  reaches the viewer on Ctrl+C; richer clipboard flavours are not bridged.
- Chromium's frame pacing is left alone by default. Measured here: the default
  60 Hz frame clock gives 60 fps repaint, 59.3 fps capture, 60 fps delivery with
  no dropped frames — the pipeline is not the limit, the frame clock is.
  `--disable-frame-rate-limit --disable-gpu-vsync` raises capture to ~114 fps but
  drives `requestAnimationFrame` to ~3240 Hz, changing every animation's timing
  for the model as well. To opt in for the next launch, create a file named
  `uncapped` in the registry directory (`~/.dsh/run/gui-browser/`); delete it to
  go back. Page restarts are needed, so the browser's current tabs are lost.
- Lossless frames are a per-viewer choice, off by default, because they cost the
  frame rate the pane exists for. Measured at 1280x720 on bilibili while it is
  being scrolled and repainted, from t

A static page emits no frames at all in either mode, and the model's own
  screenshots are a separate on-demand capture: at the same moment a full-quality
  screenshot of that page measured 203 KB as JPEG and 654 KB as PNG, so the
  mirror's encoding never touches what the model sees. Those figures are for a
  full-size cast; because the cast now follows the pane, lossless costs a narrow
  pane far less than the table suggests — measured the same way, a 160x90
  screencast held 60 fps at 2 KB a frame and 1.2 Mbit/s.
